# Diverticulosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Diverticulosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/1S02A2)

---

## Summary

Diverticulosis is a type of <u>diverticular disease</u> that consists of the formation of abnormal outpouchings of the <u>colonic</u> <u>mucosa</u> (<u>diverticula</u>). These can develop due to a combination of chronically elevated intraluminal pressures due to chronic <u>constipation</u> (e.g., due to low-fiber diets, lack of physical exercise) and age-related weakening of <u>connective tissue</u>. This typically causes the <u>colonic</u> <u>mucosa</u> to herniate through areas of <u>weakness</u> in the muscular layer. The <u>sigmoid colon</u> is most commonly involved. <u>Incidence</u> increases with age, and approx. 50% of individuals are affected by the 7<sup>th</sup> decade of life. Diverticulosis is typically asymptomatic but occasionally presents with altered bowel habits and/or abdominal discomfort. It is often an incidental finding during the diagnostic evaluation of abdominal <u>pain</u> and other gastrointestinal conditions. <u>Colonoscopy</u> is the diagnostic modality of choice for symptomatic diverticulosis but is contraindicated if <u>acute inflammation</u> of the <u>diverticula</u> (i.e., <u>diverticulitis</u>) is suspected. Management is typically aimed at preventing disease progression and treating complications, e.g., <u>diverticulitis</u>, painless <u>diverticular bleeding</u> (an important cause of severe <u>lower GI bleeding</u>), and <u>diverticular disease</u>-associated <u>colitis</u> (<u>chronic inflammation</u> of <u>diverticula</u> and surrounding <u>colonic</u> <u>mucosa</u>).




See also “<u>Diverticulitis</u>.”

---

## Definitions

* <u>Diverticula</u>: blind pouches that protrude from the gastrointestinal wall and communicate with the lumen 

* True diverticulum; : a type of diverticulum that affects all layers of the intestinal wall.

* Rare (except <u>Meckel diverticulum</u> )

* Typically congenital

* Most commonly occur in the <u>cecum</u>

* Occur less commonly in the <u>colon</u>

* <u>False diverticulum</u> or pseudodiverticulum: type of diverticulum that involves only the <u>mucosa</u> and <u>submucosa</u> and does not contain muscular layer or adventitia.

* Most common type of gastrointestinal <u>diverticula</u>

* Typically acquired

* Localized particularly in the <u>sigmoid colon</u>

* Diverticulosis: the presence of multiple <u>colonic</u> <u>diverticula</u> without evidence of infection [[1]](/library/c_YaM7)





![True diverticula and pseudodiverticula](media/w3eci4srrpy2d5ksxr907azu.jpg)

---

## Epidemiology

* In the US, ∼ 50% of individuals > 60 years have diverticulosis [[2]](/library/DOb1uF)

* More common in high-income countries due to the higher <u>prevalence</u> of a high-fat, low-fiber diet




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Caused mainly by lifestyle and environmental factors

* Diet (low-fiber, rich in fat and red meat)

* <u>Obesity</u>

* Low physical activity

* Increasing age

* Smoking

* Intestinal microbiome

* Other causes: genetic factors

* <u>Connective tissue disorders</u> (e.g., <u>Marfan syndrome</u>, <u>Ehler-Danlos syndrome</u>) [[1]](/library/c_YaM7)[[3]](/library/d_YoM7)

* <u>Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease</u>





References:[[4]](/library/_S05Xf)[[5]](/library/-S0DXf)

---

## Pathophysiology

The formation of <u>diverticula</u> is considered multifactorial.




* Increased intraluminal pressure, e.g., due to chronic <u>constipation</u>

* <u>Weakness</u> of the intestinal wall

* Age-related loss of elasticity of the <u>connective tissue</u>

* Physiological gaps in the intestinal wall, which occur where <u>blood vessels</u> penetrate, predispose to protrusion and <u>herniation</u> of intestinal <u>mucosa</u> and <u>submucosa</u>.

---

## Clinical features

* Usually asymptomatic

* May manifest with abdominal discomfort or <u>pain</u>, especially if associated with chronic <u>constipation</u>  [[6]](/library/Emc8h10)

* <u>Diverticular bleeding</u>  [[7]](/library/dqXox_)

---

## Diagnosis

### Asymptomatic diverticulosis [[8]](/library/W_YPM7)




* Typically an incidental diagnosis

* No workup required





### Symptomatic diverticulosis [[9]](/library/4ab3kH)[[10]](/library/AdbRss)[[11]](/library/CIYqUq)[[12]](/library/7db4rs)[[13]](/library/9dbNHs)




* <u>Colonoscopy</u>: diagnostic modality of choice for suspected symptomatic diverticulosis    [[12]](/library/7db4rs)

* Indications

* <u>Lower GI bleed</u>

* <u>Recurrent abdominal pain</u> and/or <u>diarrhea</u>

* Concern for underlying <u>malignancy</u>  [[13]](/library/9dbNHs)

* Findings: well-defined outpouching from the <u>colonic</u> wall

* Avoid if acute <u>diverticulitis</u> is suspected.

* <u>Biopsy</u> and histological analysis can be performed, if necessary

* <u>Double-contrast barium enema</u>: highly sensitive test to detect diverticulosis but not commonly performed  [[9]](/library/4ab3kH)

* Consider in the workup of the following: [[10]](/library/AdbRss)

* Recurrent <u>LLQ</u> <u>pain</u> without <u>signs of acute inflammation</u>

* Altered bowel habits

* <u>Lower GI bleed</u> in a hemodynamically stable patient if <u>colonoscopy</u> cannot be performed

* Contraindications: suspected <u>diverticulitis</u> or perforated diverticulum  [[11]](/library/CIYqUq)[[13]](/library/9dbNHs)

* Findings: outpouching of the <u>colonic</u> wall of variable size

* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>

* Indications: may be performed as part of the workup for nonspecific <u>LLQ</u> <u>pain</u> [[11]](/library/CIYqUq)

* Findings: <u>hypoechoic</u> or <u>anechoic</u> outpouching from the <u>colonic</u> wall [[13]](/library/9dbNHs)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Colonoscopy</u> is the diagnostic modality of choice for symptomatic diverticulosis.

## Treatment

* Asymptomatic diverticulosis

* No treatment can reverse the growth of existing <u>diverticula</u>.

* The goal is the prevention of progression (see “Prevention”).

* Symptomatic uncomplicated <u>diverticular disease</u>: unclear  [[6]](/library/Emc8h10)[[12]](/library/7db4rs)

* Complicated <u>diverticular disease</u> (e.g., <u>diverticulitis</u>): See “Complications.”

---

## Prevention

Consider the following measures to prevent disease progression and development of complications. See “<u>Management of diverticulitis</u>” for <u>secondary prevention</u> of recurrent <u>diverticulitis</u>. [[14]](/library/pJYLEJ)[[[15]](/library/ohc0UX0)




* Dietary modification, e.g., high-fiber diet, <u>DASH diet</u>, or <u>vegetarian diet</u>  [[16]](/library/dScoAb0)

* Weight reduction

* Vigorous physical activity

* <u>Smoking cessation</u>

* <u>Treatment of alcoholism</u>

---

## Complications

* Diverticular bleeding [[17]](/library/o_Y067)[[18]](/library/4R03Mf)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Diverticulosis is the most common cause of lower <u>GI bleeding</u> in adults.

* Occurs in ∼ 5% of individuals with diverticulosis

* Etiology: <u>erosions</u> around the edge of <u>diverticula</u>

* Clinical findings

* Painless <u>hematochezia</u>

* <u>Signs of anemia</u> may be present if recurrent

* Severe or ongoing bleeding: significant drop in <u>hemoglobin</u> → <u>hemodynamic instability</u> (<u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, reduced <u>level of consciousness</u>)

* In 70–80% of cases, bleeding ceases spontaneously

* Differential diagnosis: other causes of <u>lower gastrointestinal bleeding</u> (e.g., hemorrhoidal bleeding)

* Treatment: See “<u>Initial management of overt GI bleeding</u>.”

* <u>Endoscopic hemostasis</u> during <u>colonoscopy</u> (e.g., <u>epinephrine</u> injection, thermal coagulation, ligation)

* <u>Angiography</u> with vessel embolization

* <u>Acute inflammation</u>: i.e., <u>diverticulitis</u>

* Clinical features include <u>left lower quadrant</u> <u>pain</u>, low-grade <u>fever</u>, tender palpable mass, change in bowel habits

* Downstream complications include <u>GI perforation</u>, <u>abscess</u>, <u>fistula</u>, <u>intestinal obstruction</u>, and <u>pylephlebitis</u>. [[17]](/library/o_Y067)

* <u>Chronic inflammation</u>: <u>Diverticular disease</u>-associated <u>colitis</u> (<u>DAC</u>), also called diverticular <u>colitis</u> or segmental <u>colitis</u> associated with diverticulosis (<u>SCAD</u>)  [[19]](/library/1mc2e10)

* Multifactorial inflammation of segments of <u>colonic</u> <u>mucosa</u> and <u>diverticula</u>

* May overlap with <u>IBD</u> and is treated similarly to <u>Crohn disease</u>
